title: Aim Statement & Measurement Plan — Sepsis Pathway 2.0
text:
# Aim Statement & Measurement Plan — Sepsis Pathway 2.0

**Date:** January 28, 2026
**Author:** Karen Holloway, MD (VP Quality) with Sandra Pell (Quality Data Analyst)
**Status:** Approved by Sepsis Steering Committee as the measurement plan of record

---

## Aim Statement

Within two quarters of go-live, Stillwater Regional will improve adult sepsis care such that:

| # | Metric | Baseline (Q4 2025) | Target |
|---|---|---|---|
| M1 | CMS SEP-1 3-hour bundle compliance | *disputed — see note* | ≥ 90% |
| M2 | Median ED door-to-antibiotic time, suspected septic shock | ~155 min | < 60 min |
| M3 | Nurse-driven sepsis screening completion (ED + 4West) | not measured | ≥ 95% |
| M4 | Risk-adjusted sepsis mortality (O:E ratio) | 1.18 | relative 20% reduction |

## Note on the M1 baseline

The committee could not agree on a single baseline figure for SEP-1 3-hour bundle compliance. Two measurement methods are in use and produce materially different numbers (manual chart abstraction vs. the automated EHR SEP-1 flag). The measurement & analytics workstream is tasked with reconciling the two methods before go-live. **Until reconciled, M1 is reported as a range and no single baseline is endorsed.** This is the most important open measurement question in the initiative.

## Measurement cadence

- Manual SEP-1 abstraction: monthly, on a 30-chart random sample (Quality Dept).
- Automated EHR SEP-1 dashboard: continuous (Clinical Informatics).
- Mortality (O:E): quarterly, risk-adjusted via the existing vendor model; not powered for short-window pilot inference.

## Caveat carried forward

Mortality (M4) is a lagging, low-frequency outcome. The committee agreed in advance that the pilot window will be **too short and too small to support any statistical claim about mortality change**, and that mortality results from the pilot are to be reported as descriptive only, not as evidence of effect.

title: Quality Improvement Charter — Sepsis Pathway 2.0
text:
# Quality Improvement Charter — Sepsis Pathway 2.0

**Date:** January 26, 2026
**Sponsor:** Yusuf Adeyemi, MD — Chief Medical Officer
**Initiative Lead:** Karen Holloway, MD — VP, Quality & Patient Safety
**Facility:** Stillwater Regional Medical Center (412-bed community teaching hospital, Calhoun County)

---

## Background & Trigger

On January 12, 2026, a sentinel event review was opened following the in-hospital death of an adult patient who presented to the Emergency Department with undifferentiated infection and deteriorated to septic shock. Preliminary review indicated delays in sepsis recognition and antibiotic administration relative to our existing Sepsis Response Protocol (v1.0, effective June 2024).

A retrospective look-back at the prior quarter (Q4 2025) was commissioned as part of the root-cause analysis. Early findings identified **three preventable sepsis-related deaths** associated with bundle-compliance failures. (Note: the death-attribution count is under active review by the RCA team and should be treated as preliminary pending the final report.)

## Aim

Redesign the adult sepsis-response pathway end-to-end ("Sepsis Pathway 2.0") to improve early recognition, shorten time to antibiotics, raise CMS SEP-1 bundle compliance, and reduce risk-adjusted sepsis mortality.

## Scope

- **In scope:** Adult (≥18) patients with suspected sepsis or septic shock presenting to the ED or identified on inpatient units 4West and the ICU.
- **Out of scope:** Pediatric and neonatal sepsis (governed separately by the Pediatrics service line); obstetric sepsis.

## Workstreams & Owners

1. Screening & recognition — Janet Mwangi, RN (Nursing Director / Sepsis Coordinator)
2. Antibiotic timing & stewardship — Marcus Tran, MD (ED Medical Director) and Elena Soto, MD (Infectious Disease / Antimicrobial Stewardship)
3. Measurement & analytics — Sandra Pell (Quality Data Analyst) and David Lin (Clinical Informatics)
4. Escalation & critical care — Priyanka Rao, MD (ICU Director)
5. Medication & supply — Tom Becker, PharmD (Pharmacy Director)

## Governance

The Sepsis Steering Committee reports to the Quality & Patient Safety Committee, which holds final approval authority over any protocol change. Board Quality Committee receives a summary at quarter close.

## Target Timeline

RCA final report by end of February; redesigned protocol drafted in March; pilot on 4West and the ED through April; Quality Committee decision in April; phased house-wide rollout thereafter.

title: SEP-1 Bundle Compliance — Manual Chart Abstraction (Quality Dept)
text:
# SEP-1 Bundle Compliance — Manual Chart Abstraction (Quality Dept)

**Date:** February 20, 2026
**Analyst:** Sandra Pell, Quality Data Analyst
**Method:** Manual abstraction per CMS SEP-1 specifications, random 30-chart sample (Q4 2025 adult sepsis cases)

---

## Headline

**SEP-1 3-hour bundle compliance: 62%** (18 of 29 abstractable charts; 1 excluded as non-sepsis on review).

This is the figure I am submitting as the official Quality Department baseline, computed strictly to CMS abstraction rules.

## Why this is lower than the dashboard number

Clinical Informatics' EHR dashboard reports **84%** for what looks like the same measure. The numbers are not comparable, and the difference is not an error in either system — it is a definition difference:

- **Manual abstraction (this report, 62%)** applies the full CMS SEP-1 "all-or-none" logic: a case fails if *any* element (lactate, blood cultures before antibiotics, broad-spectrum antibiotics within 3h, repeat lactate where indicated, timely fluids) is missed or late. It also applies CMS time-zero rules strictly.
- **EHR automated flag (dashboard, 84%)** counts a case as compliant when the *antibiotic order is placed* in the sepsis order set. It does not verify that every bundle element was completed on time, and it uses order-placement time rather than administration time.

So the dashboard measures "bundle *initiated*," and abstraction measures "bundle *completed to spec*." They will not converge without a definition change.

## Recommendation

The committee should pick ONE method of record before go-live. I recommend manual abstraction for any externally reported or board-reported figure, because that is what CMS will hold us to. The EHR flag is useful for real-time prompting but should not be reported as the compliance rate.

*(This divergence remained unresolved as of protocol approval in April.)*

title: Pilot Interim Report — Sepsis Pathway 2.0 (ED + 4West)
text:
# Pilot Interim Report — Sepsis Pathway 2.0 (ED + 4West)

**Date:** April 8, 2026
**Status:** INTERIM / PROVISIONAL — descriptive only; not a final result
**Author:** Sandra Pell (Quality) with Janet Mwangi, RN
**Pilot window:** February 24 – April 6, 2026 (6 weeks), ED and unit 4West

---

## What we piloted

The v2.0 elements ahead of formal approval: mandatory nurse-driven screening, the charge-nurse sepsis pager, stratified antibiotic timing, and the 3-hour repeat-lactate trigger.

## Process measures (encouraging)

- Nurse screening completion (ED): 41% → **~88%**.
- Median door-to-antibiotic, suspected septic shock: 155 min → **~74 min** (target < 60 min; trending toward it).
- Repeat-lactate ordered where indicated: 38% → **~80%**.

These process gains are real and consistent with the design intent.

## Mortality (NOT a result)

During the 6-week pilot there were **4 sepsis deaths among 71 pilot-eligible cases**, versus a comparable prior-period rate that would have predicted ~5–6. **This looks lower, but we cannot and do not claim a mortality effect.** Reasons, stated plainly:

- The sample is tiny (71 cases, 4 events). The confidence interval is enormous.
- Six weeks spans a seasonal decline in respiratory sepsis; the comparison period was mid-winter.
- Case mix was not risk-adjusted in this interim cut.
- The aim statement pre-committed to treating pilot mortality as descriptive only.

**Bottom line: the pilot does not demonstrate, and is not capable of demonstrating, a mortality reduction.** Anyone citing a mortality benefit from this pilot is over-reading the data. A powered O:E read will take several quarters post-go-live.

## Recommendation

Proceed to approval on the strength of the **process** improvements and the RCA findings, not on mortality.

title: Final Root Cause Analysis — Sentinel Event SE-2026-003
text:
# Final Root Cause Analysis — Sentinel Event SE-2026-003

**Date:** February 27, 2026
**Status:** FINAL — supersedes the Preliminary RCA of February 9, 2026
**Facilitator:** Karen Holloway, MD (VP Quality)
**Review panel:** Holloway, Tran (ED), Rao (ICU), Soto (ID), Mwangi (Nursing), Becker (Pharmacy)

---

## 1. Scope

Root-cause analysis of the January 12, 2026 adult sepsis death (SE-2026-003), with a Q4 2025 look-back to determine whether the event reflected a systemic pattern.

## 2. Corrected death attribution

The preliminary report cited three Q4 2025 sepsis deaths with bundle-compliance failures. On case-by-case adjudication the panel **reclassified one of the three**: that patient had a documented DNR and a comfort-focused goals-of-care order in place before the sepsis episode, and the death was determined to be **expected and not attributable** to bundle failure.

**Final determination: two (2) attributable, potentially preventable sepsis deaths** in Q4 2025, plus the January index event. The "three deaths" figure from the preliminary report should not be cited; it was superseded by this adjudication.

## 3. Contributing factors (final)

1. **Recognition gap.** Nurse-driven screening was optional under Protocol v1.0 and was not performed in 2 of the 3 index/look-back cases.
2. **Antibiotic delay.** Door-to-antibiotic time exceeded the 3-hour target in the index case (≈3h40m) and in one look-back case.
3. **No deterioration trigger.** Absence of a repeat-lactate requirement delayed recognition of progression to shock.
4. **Infusion delay (one case).** In one look-back case, antibiotic infusion was delayed by an infusion-pump programming issue; this finding prompted the pharmacy review that later intersected with the Veramed VX-200 field alert (see Pharmacy correspondence, March 2026).

## 4. Recommendations

- Mandate nurse-driven screening (adopted in Protocol v2.0).
- Stratified antibiotic timing with a 1-hour target for septic shock (adopted in v2.0; see stewardship memo for the non-shock rationale).
- Add a repeat-lactate trigger at 3 hours (adopted in v2.0).
- Reconcile the two SEP-1 compliance measurement methods before go-live (open).

## 5. Note on measurement

The panel was unable to state a single SEP-1 baseline compliance figure because the manual-abstraction and automated-EHR methods disagree materially. This is flagged as an unresolved measurement issue, not a finding of fact.

title: Preliminary Root Cause Analysis — Sentinel Event SE-2026-003
text:
# Preliminary Root Cause Analysis — Sentinel Event SE-2026-003

**Date:** February 9, 2026
**Status:** PRELIMINARY — not for distribution outside the RCA team; superseded by the final report
**Facilitator:** Karen Holloway, MD (VP Quality)
**Event:** Adult sepsis death, ED, January 12, 2026

---

## Summary

This preliminary analysis is issued at the two-week mark to orient the Sepsis Steering Committee. **Figures here are provisional and will change in the final report.**

## Index event

The index patient presented with fever, tachycardia, and hypotension and was not screened with the nurse-driven tool at triage. Antibiotics were administered approximately 3 hours 40 minutes after arrival. The patient progressed to refractory septic shock and died on hospital day 2.

## Q4 2025 look-back (provisional)

To establish whether the index event was isolated, the team reviewed adult sepsis deaths in Q4 2025. The provisional review identified **three (3) sepsis-related deaths associated with documented bundle-compliance failures** (missed or late antibiotics, no repeat lactate, or no screening). All three are being treated, at this preliminary stage, as potentially preventable.

> ⚠️ Caveat: attribution is not final. At least one of the three cases involved a documented goals-of-care limitation (DNR / comfort-focused care) that may make the death non-attributable to bundle failure. The final report will adjudicate each case.

## Provisional contributing factors

1. Screening not performed / not mandatory under Protocol v1.0.
2. Antibiotic administration beyond the 3-hour target.
3. No repeat-lactate trigger to catch deterioration.

## Next steps

Case-by-case attribution adjudication; interview ED and nursing staff; reconcile the timeline against the EHR audit log. Final report targeted for end of February.

title: Email: Manual SEP-1 audit done — and we have a measurement problem
text:
# Email: Manual SEP-1 audit done — and we have a measurement problem

**From:** Sandra Pell
**To:** Karen Holloway
**Cc:** David Lin
**Sent:** February 20, 2026, 4:48 PM
**Subject:** Manual SEP-1 audit done — and we have a measurement problem

---

Karen,

Manual abstraction is finished. Strict CMS all-or-none on a 30-chart Q4 sample: **62% 3-hour bundle compliance** (18 of 29 abstractable; one excluded as non-sepsis). Full memo to follow.

Here's the problem: David's EHR dashboard reports **84%** for what people *think* is the same measure. It isn't. The dashboard counts a case as compliant when the antibiotic is *ordered* in the sepsis order set. Abstraction fails a case if any element is missed or late, and uses administration time, not order time. So one is "bundle initiated" and the other is "bundle completed to spec." They will never agree.

We need the committee to pick ONE method of record before go-live. My recommendation: report manual abstraction for anything board- or CMS-facing, because that's the standard we're actually held to. Happy to walk through it.

Sandra

title: Email: Re: Manual SEP-1 audit — the 84% isn't wrong either
text:
# Email: Re: Manual SEP-1 audit — the 84% isn't wrong either

**From:** David Lin
**To:** Sandra Pell, Karen Holloway
**Sent:** February 22, 2026, 9:32 AM
**Subject:** Re: Manual SEP-1 audit — the 84% isn't wrong either

---

Agreed that 62% and 84% measure different things — but I want to push back on "report manual only."

The EHR flag isn't an error and it isn't vanity. It's what drives the real-time prompt at the bedside: when it fires, a nurse sees it and acts. If we bury it and only ever cite the abstraction number, we lose the live behavioral lever. The 84% tells us how often the *order set* is being used; the 62% tells us how often we *complete to CMS spec*. Both are true.

My proposal: report 62% (manual) as the official compliance rate — Sandra's right that CMS holds us to all-or-none — but keep the 84% on the operational dashboard, clearly labeled "bundle initiation, not SEP-1 completion," so nobody confuses them again.

I'll relabel the dashboard today so the definition is unmissable. But I don't think we've actually *reconciled* anything — we've just agreed they're different. The single defensible baseline question is still open.

David

title: Email: Antibiotic timing — we should commit to 1 hour
text:
# Email: Antibiotic timing — we should commit to 1 hour

**From:** Marcus Tran
**To:** Sepsis Steering Committee
**Sent:** March 2, 2026, 7:05 PM
**Subject:** Antibiotic timing — we should commit to 1 hour

---

Colleagues,

I want to make the case plainly: our antibiotic timing target should be **one hour, door to antibiotic, for every patient we suspect of sepsis.**

The evidence on this is, to me, overwhelming — every hour of delay to effective antibiotics is associated with higher mortality. Our own sentinel case waited nearly four hours and died. The 3-hour target in v1.0 is, functionally, permission to be slow. If we set the bar at one hour for everyone, we will save lives, and the measurement is dead simple: one clock, one number, no carve-outs.

I know stewardship will worry about over-treatment. I respect that. But I'd rather give an extra dose of antibiotics to someone who didn't need it than lose another patient because we were debating whether they met "shock" criteria while the clock ran. Speed first; de-escalate later.

Let's commit to a universal 1-hour target in v2.0.

Marcus

title: Email: Stewardship position on the 1-hour proposal (memo attached)
text:
# Email: Stewardship position on the 1-hour proposal (memo attached)

**From:** Elena Soto
**To:** Sepsis Steering Committee
**Sent:** March 6, 2026, 11:20 AM
**Subject:** Stewardship position on the 1-hour proposal (memo attached)

---

Marcus, all,

I've attached my formal stewardship position memo. I want it on the record before we finalize.

Short version: **one hour for septic shock, yes. A blanket one-hour broad-spectrum mandate for everyone we "suspect," no.** The mortality evidence Marcus cites is robust for shock and weak-to-absent for sepsis without shock. A universal 1-hour clock, enforced as a metric, reliably drives broad-spectrum overuse, *C. diff*, and antibiotics-before-cultures — real harms, for a benefit that isn't demonstrated in the non-shock group.

"Give the extra dose, de-escalate later" sounds harmless but it isn't free, and at scale it's how stewardship programs lose the resistance fight.

My recommendation is to **stratify**: 1-hour for shock, 3-hour for sepsis without shock with stewardship-guided selection. I'll support v2.0 enthusiastically if it stratifies, and I'll file a formal dissent if it imposes a universal 1-hour mandate. The evidence briefing I circulated Feb 1 lays out the citations.

Elena

title: Email: Veramed VX-200 pump — voluntary recall, action needed
text:
# Email: Veramed VX-200 pump — voluntary recall, action needed

**From:** Tom Becker
**To:** Sepsis Steering Committee
**Cc:** Yusuf Adeyemi
**Sent:** March 31, 2026, 8:55 AM
**Subject:** Veramed VX-200 pump — voluntary recall, action needed

---

All,

Following up on the field safety alert Veramed sent March 5: as of March 30 they have escalated to a **voluntary recall** of the VX-200 infusion pump. The issue is an over-infusion risk when a specific guardrail setting is bypassed — low probability, but they're pulling them.

What this means for us:
- The VX-200 is our standard smart pump on the ED and 4West. We have ~140 affected units.
- **Interim:** for time-critical sepsis antibiotics, pharmacy and nursing will use the backup pump pool and, where necessary, supervised manual administration, until swaps are complete. I've briefed the charge nurses.
- **Replacement:** Veramed is shipping VX-210 units; full swap expected by early May.

Relevant to our RCA: one Q4 look-back case had an antibiotic infusion delayed by a pump programming problem. So this isn't only a device-safety issue — it intersects directly with our door-to-antibiotic goal. I'll keep the committee updated as the swap proceeds. The field alert is now superseded by the recall notice; treat the recall as the current guidance.

Tom

title: Email: Escalation policy — we're going with the charge-nurse pager
text:
# Email: Escalation policy — we're going with the charge-nurse pager

**From:** Karen Holloway
**To:** Sepsis Steering Committee
**Sent:** April 2, 2026, 3:30 PM
**Subject:** Escalation policy — we're going with the charge-nurse pager

---

Team,

Decision on the escalation mechanism, so we can lock v2.0 §6.

Priyanka and Janet's March 20 draft proposed a dedicated sepsis nurse, one per shift on the ED and 4West. I took it to the Staffing Committee. Under the FY2026 position-control freeze (Nurse Staffing Policy HR-NS-002), ~6 net-new FTE is not fundable this cycle, and the CNO/CFO declined to sponsor an in-year exception.

So we're adopting the alternative: **the charge nurse carries the sepsis-alert pager** on each shift. No net-new FTE. It's a weaker form of single-point accountability — the charge nurse carries it alongside everything else — and I want that trade-off named, not buried. If the pilot shows the pager isn't enough, we make the dedicated-role case again in the FY2027 budget.

The adopted memo is finalized (April 1) and folds into Protocol v2.0 §6. The dedicated-nurse draft is now superseded.

Karen

title: Email: Veramed Field Safety Notice — VX-200 Infusion Pump (FSN-2026-014)
text:
# Email: Veramed Field Safety Notice — VX-200 Infusion Pump (FSN-2026-014)

**From:** Veramed Systems — Field Safety
**To:** Tom Becker (Pharmacy Director, Stillwater Regional)
**Sent:** March 5, 2026, 10:12 AM
**Subject:** URGENT Field Safety Notice — VX-200 Infusion Pump (FSN-2026-014)

---

Dear Mr. Becker,

This Field Safety Notice concerns the **Veramed VX-200 Infusion Pump**. We have identified a condition in which, **if the dose-error-reduction guardrail is manually bypassed**, the pump may under-rare circumstances deliver an infusion at a rate higher than programmed.

**Recommended interim action (this notice):**
- Do **not** bypass the guardrail/limit settings on VX-200 pumps.
- Continue normal use with guardrails enabled; risk is associated only with the bypass condition.
- No device return is required at this time.

This is a precautionary notice, not a recall. We are continuing our investigation and will advise if our guidance changes. A corrective action may follow.

Please cascade to nursing and biomed.

Veramed Systems, Field Safety Team

---

*[Internal note appended by T. Becker, 2026-03-06: "Reviewed. Guardrail-bypass is rare in our workflow but not impossible during rapid sepsis dosing. Watching this. — TB"]*

title: Email: Veramed VOLUNTARY RECALL — VX-200 Infusion Pump (supersedes FSN-2026-014)
text:
# Email: Veramed VOLUNTARY RECALL — VX-200 Infusion Pump (supersedes FSN-2026-014)

**From:** Veramed Systems — Field Safety
**To:** Tom Becker (Pharmacy Director, Stillwater Regional)
**Sent:** March 30, 2026, 2:40 PM
**Subject:** VOLUNTARY RECALL — VX-200 Infusion Pump (supersedes FSN-2026-014)

---

Dear Mr. Becker,

This notice **supersedes our Field Safety Notice FSN-2026-014 of March 5**. Following completion of our investigation, Veramed is initiating a **voluntary recall** of the VX-200 Infusion Pump.

**Current guidance (this recall notice is now the operative instruction):**
- The earlier "continue use with guardrails enabled" guidance is withdrawn.
- Affected VX-200 units should be transitioned out of service for time-critical infusions as replacement inventory allows.
- Veramed will supply **VX-210** replacement units. For your site (~140 units), shipment is scheduled to complete by **early May 2026**.
- Where immediate replacement is not yet available, use alternative pumps or institutional backup procedures for critical infusions.

We recognize the operational impact and have prioritized your account given your sepsis time-to-antibiotic program. Your Veramed account manager will coordinate the swap schedule.

Veramed Systems, Field Safety Team

title: Meeting 001: Sepsis Pathway 2.0 — Steering Committee Kickoff
text:
# Meeting 001: Sepsis Pathway 2.0 — Steering Committee Kickoff

**Date:** January 30, 2026
**Location:** Boardroom B
**Attendees:** Karen Holloway (Lead), Yusuf Adeyemi (CMO, sponsor), Marcus Tran (ED), Priyanka Rao (ICU), Elena Soto (ID/Stewardship), Janet Mwangi (Nursing), Tom Becker (Pharmacy), Sandra Pell (Quality), David Lin (Informatics)
**Duration:** 60 minutes

---

[12:02] Holloway: Thanks all. Yusuf will say a word, then we go around for current-state reads. No solutions yet — I want the problem clear first.

[12:04] Adeyemi: Briefly. A patient died of sepsis in our ED who, on first review, shouldn't have. This is not about blame. It's about a system that let antibiotics run nearly four hours and didn't screen at triage. We fix the system. The board is watching, and so is the accreditor, but that's not why we do it.

[12:08] Holloway: Janet, screening?

[12:09] Mwangi: Honest answer — screening is optional today and it shows. At triage it gets done when it's not busy and skipped when it's slammed. If you asked me to guess our bundle compliance, I'd say maybe seventy percent? It *feels* like we get it right most of the time but not always. I don't have a hard number; that's Sandra and David's job.

[12:13] Holloway: And that's the second problem — we don't agree on the number. Sandra?

[12:14] Pell: Right. I'm running a strict manual abstraction on a Q4 sample. David has an automated dashboard. I'll just flag now: I expect them to disagree, maybe a lot, because they're not measuring the same thing. We'll bring you both and a recommendation.

[12:16] Tran: Can I name the thing I care about? Time to antibiotics. Three hours is too slow. I'll be advocating to tighten it hard. Every hour matters.

[12:17] Soto: And I'll be the one saying "for which patients?" I'm not against speed. I'm against a blanket mandate that has us pouring carbapenems into people who aren't infected. We'll have that fight productively, Marcus.

[12:18] Tran: Looking forward to it.

[12:19] Rao: From critical care — by the time they reach me it's often already shock, and the upstream delay is baked in. I care most about the recognition-to-escalation handoff. Right now there's no standing alert; it's whoever picks up the phone.

[12:21] Becker: Pharmacy: stocking is fine, but I'll watch our infusion devices. We had at least one case where the pump, not the order, was the delay. I want to keep an eye on that.

[12:23] Holloway: Good. That's the map: recognition, timing, measurement, escalation, supply. Final RCA end of February. Sandra and David, the single defensible compliance number is your first deliverable. Everyone come to the design workshop in March ready to argue from evidence, not vibes.

[12:26] Adeyemi: One rule from me: until the final RCA, the "three deaths" figure stays in this room. It's preliminary. We don't repeat preliminary numbers.

[12:27] Holloway: Agreed. Thank you all.

title: Meeting 002: Morbidity & Mortality Conference — SE-2026-003
text:
# Meeting 002: Morbidity & Mortality Conference — SE-2026-003

**Date:** February 25, 2026
**Location:** Auditorium
**Attendees:** Karen Holloway (facilitator), Marcus Tran (ED), Priyanka Rao (ICU), Elena Soto (ID), Janet Mwangi (Nursing), plus department staff
**Format:** Closed peer-review M&M (non-punitive)

---

[07:03] Holloway: This is peer review, non-punitive, privileged. We're reviewing the January 12 case and the three Q4 look-back cases the preliminary RCA flagged. The final report is being written now; what we say here informs it.

[07:07] Tran: The index case is clear. No triage screen, antibiotics at three hours forty, progressed to shock, died day two. If we'd screened and dosed at one hour, different story. That's the case for moving fast.

[07:10] Rao: I don't disagree on the index case. I want to talk about the three look-back cases, because I don't think they're all the same. One of them — the 78-year-old — had a DNR and a comfort-care order in the chart from before the sepsis episode. That patient was not going to the ICU regardless of bundle timing. Calling that death "preventable" because a lactate was late isn't honest.

[07:13] Holloway: That's an important distinction for the final report. Sandra's adjudicating each case. Priyanka, can you put that in writing for the RCA team?

[07:14] Rao: Yes. My read is two attributable, not three. The comfort-care case shouldn't be in the preventable column.

[07:16] Soto: On the index case — was it actually shock on arrival, or did it become shock? Because that changes what the "right" antibiotic timing even was. If it wasn't shock at presentation, a one-hour mandate wouldn't necessarily have changed the antibiotic, just started the clock earlier. I'm not minimizing it. I'm saying "one hour for everyone" isn't the clean lesson some will want to draw from this.

[07:19] Tran: Or it's exactly the lesson. We waited because we were unsure, and being unsure killed time.

[07:20] Soto: Being unsure is also when you do harm by reflexively broad-spectrum dosing people who turn out to have heart failure or a PE. We'll have this out at the workshop.

[07:22] Mwangi: The thread through all of these is recognition. Nobody screened. If the screen is mandatory and it fires, the timing argument largely takes care of itself, because the clock starts when it should.

[07:25] Holloway: That's the consensus I'm hearing — recognition first, and the timing target stratified by severity, which is the workshop's job. And the death count for the final report is two attributable plus the index event, pending Sandra's written adjudication. Thank you. This was exactly the discussion we needed.

title: Meeting 003: Protocol v2.0 Design Workshop
text:
# Meeting 003: Protocol v2.0 Design Workshop

**Date:** March 12, 2026
**Location:** Boardroom B
**Attendees:** Karen Holloway (facilitator), Marcus Tran (ED), Elena Soto (ID/Stewardship), Janet Mwangi (Nursing), Priyanka Rao (ICU)
**Duration:** 2 hours

---

[13:05] Holloway: Today we resolve antibiotic timing. Marcus wants one hour for everyone. Elena wants stratification. We are not leaving without a decision both of you can sign.

[13:08] Tran: My position hasn't moved. One hour, door to antibiotic, anyone we suspect of sepsis. Simple, fast, measurable, and the mortality literature backs urgency.

[13:10] Soto: The literature backs urgency *in shock*. I circulated the evidence brief — the one-hour bundle was downgraded precisely because the data for non-shock sepsis are weak. A universal one-hour broad-spectrum clock buys us *C. diff* and resistance for a benefit that isn't demonstrated outside shock. I'll dissent formally if it's universal.

[13:14] Tran: And I'll say on the record that stratifying gives people an excuse to be slow on someone who's about to crash but doesn't "officially" meet shock yet.

[13:16] Rao: That's the real risk, and it's a recognition problem, not a timing-target problem. If the screen is mandatory and fires on hypotension or lactate over four, you've identified the shock patients fast. The one-hour clock attaches to *that* trigger.

[13:19] Soto: I can live with that. One hour when the shock criteria fire — hypotension needing pressors, or lactate ≥ 4. Three hours for sepsis without those, with selection off the stewardship empiric table.

[13:21] Tran: And the screen is genuinely mandatory? Not "encouraged"?

[13:22] Mwangi: Mandatory. Discrete EHR field, every triage and every shift assessment on 4West and the ICU. If it's optional we're back where we started.

[13:24] Tran: Then I can sign stratified — one hour for shock, three for non-shock — *if* recognition is mandatory and the shock trigger is unambiguous. That addresses my "excuse to be slow" worry.

[13:26] Holloway: That's the decision. Stratified timing, mandatory screening, plus the repeat-lactate at three hours Priyanka asked for. Elena, no dissent?

[13:27] Soto: No dissent. This is the evidence-based design. Thank you, Marcus, for moving.

[13:28] Tran: Recognition was the missing piece. Fine.

[13:30] Holloway: Last thing — Sandra flagged the compliance number again. We are NOT reporting a single SEP-1 baseline until manual and EHR are reconciled. v2 will say so explicitly. Escalation mechanism is still open; I'm taking the dedicated-nurse proposal to Staffing. We'll close that separately. Good work, all.

title: Meeting 004: Quality & Patient Safety Committee — Protocol v2.0 Decision
text:
# Meeting 004: Quality & Patient Safety Committee — Protocol v2.0 Decision

**Date:** April 20, 2026
**Location:** Boardroom A
**Attendees:** Karen Holloway (presenting), Yusuf Adeyemi (CMO, chair), Marcus Tran (ED), Elena Soto (ID), Priyanka Rao (ICU), committee members
**Action:** Vote on approval of Sepsis Response Protocol v2.0

---

[12:05] Adeyemi: This is the decision meeting. Karen presents, we vote. Karen.

[12:07] Holloway: Protocol v2.0 for your approval. Four substantive changes from v1.0: mandatory nurse-driven screening; stratified antibiotic timing — one hour for septic shock, three hours for sepsis without shock; a repeat lactate at three hours when the first is ≥ 2; and a charge-nurse sepsis pager for escalation. The stratification carries ID's endorsement; there is no dissent on the committee.

[12:11] Adeyemi: The escalation — this is the pager, not the dedicated nurse?

[12:12] Holloway: Correct. The dedicated sepsis-nurse proposal was not fundable under the FY26 position-control freeze. Staffing declined the in-year exception. We adopted the charge-nurse pager and named the trade-off in the memo: weaker single-point accountability, revisit in FY27 if the pilot shows it's insufficient.

[12:15] Rao: For the record, I proposed the dedicated nurse and I still think it's better. But the pager is a defensible starting point and I support approving v2.0 with it.

[12:17] Adeyemi: Pilot results — what can we actually say?

[12:18] Holloway: Process measures improved clearly: screening from 41% to ~88%, door-to-antibiotic for shock from 155 minutes to ~74. On **mortality, we say nothing** — the pilot was not powered, the window was six weeks, and the aim statement pre-committed to treating pilot mortality as descriptive only. The interim report says this explicitly. We approve on the RCA findings and the process gains, not on mortality.

[12:21] Soto: And the compliance number?

[12:22] Holloway: Still two methods, still unreconciled. v2.0 states that compliance must be interpreted accordingly until we converge on one method of record. That work continues after go-live.

[12:24] Adeyemi: I appreciate the candor about what we don't know. Motion to approve Protocol v2.0, effective May 1. All in favor?

[12:25] *Unanimous. v2.0 approved.*

[12:26] Adeyemi: Approved. Karen, get the board summary ready for May 5. And fix the death-count slide — it should read two attributable, per the final RCA, not three.

title: Reference — CMS SEP-1 (Severe Sepsis & Septic Shock) Bundle
text:
# Reference — CMS SEP-1 (Severe Sepsis & Septic Shock) Bundle

**Date:** October 1, 2025
**Document type:** Standing reference summary (Quality Department)
**Status:** Current external requirement — stable reference, not a Stillwater work product

---

## What SEP-1 is

SEP-1 is the U.S. Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) inpatient quality measure for severe sepsis and septic shock. It is an **all-or-none** measure: a case is compliant only if *every* required element is completed within the specified window. This reference summarizes the elements; it is the durable external standard the hospital is held to and does not change with internal protocol revisions.

## 3-hour bundle (from time of presentation / "time zero")

1. Measure initial serum lactate.
2. Obtain blood cultures **before** administering antibiotics.
3. Administer broad-spectrum antibiotics.
4. Begin 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate ≥ 4 mmol/L.

## 6-hour bundle

5. Repeat lactate if the initial lactate was elevated.
6. Apply vasopressors for hypotension that does not respond to fluids (target MAP ≥ 65 mmHg).
7. Reassess volume status and tissue perfusion for persistent hypotension or initial lactate ≥ 4 mmol/L.

## Why "all-or-none" matters for measurement

Because the measure fails a case if any single element is missed or late, a strict CMS abstraction will almost always report a **lower** compliance rate than a system that counts partial or initiated bundles. Any internal dashboard that counts "antibiotic ordered" is measuring something different from SEP-1 and is not directly comparable. This standard is what an external reviewer (e.g., CMS, or an accreditor reviewing sepsis care) will apply.

title: Evidence Landscape — Time-to-Antibiotics in Sepsis
text:
# Evidence Landscape — Time-to-Antibiotics in Sepsis

**Date:** February 1, 2026
**Compiled by:** Elena Soto, MD (ID/Stewardship) for the Sepsis Steering Committee
**Document type:** Internal evidence briefing (reference)

---

## Purpose

Summarize, neutrally, what the literature does and does not support about antibiotic timing in sepsis, so the committee designs the protocol from evidence rather than slogans.

## What is well supported

- In **septic shock**, each hour of delay to effective antibiotics is associated with increased mortality in multiple observational cohorts. Urgency here is justified.
- Early **source control** and appropriate empiric selection matter as much as raw speed.

## What is contested

- The **"1-hour bundle"** (Surviving Sepsis Campaign, 2018/2021) was widely criticized and is not universally endorsed. The strong recommendation was downgraded in places precisely because the evidence base for a 1-hour clock in *all* sepsis is weak.
- For **sepsis without shock**, there is **no high-quality evidence** that a 1-hour antibiotic target reduces mortality relative to a 3-hour target. The marginal patients in a 1-hour mandate are disproportionately those who are *not* infected.

## Documented downsides of a universal time-to-antibiotic metric

- Increased broad-spectrum exposure and *C. difficile* risk.
- Pressure to administer antibiotics before blood cultures or adequate assessment.
- Diagnostic anchoring on infection.

## Implication for protocol design

The evidence supports *stratification*: urgency proportional to severity (1-hour for shock; a measured 3-hour pathway for non-shock sepsis with stewardship-guided selection). It does not support a single universal 1-hour broad-spectrum mandate.

title: Board Quality Committee — Sepsis Pathway 2.0 Summary
text:
# Board Quality Committee — Sepsis Pathway 2.0 Summary

**Date:** May 5, 2026
**Prepared for:** Board Quality Committee, Q1 close
**Prepared by:** Yusuf Adeyemi, MD (CMO) and Karen Holloway, MD (VP Quality)

---

## Executive summary

Following a January sentinel event, Stillwater Regional chartered Sepsis Pathway 2.0, a cross-functional redesign of adult sepsis care. The Quality & Patient Safety Committee approved the redesigned protocol (v2.0) on April 20; it takes effect May 1.

## Quality highlights (board slide)

- **Root-cause analysis identified 3 preventable sepsis deaths** and significant gaps in screening and antibiotic timing.
- Redesigned protocol mandates nurse-driven screening, stratified antibiotic timing (1-hour for septic shock), and a repeat-lactate trigger.
- Pilot on the ED and 4West showed improved process compliance.

> Editorial note for the board packet: the "3 deaths" bullet is carried over from the **preliminary** RCA. The **final** RCA (Feb 27) adjudicated this down to **2 attributable deaths** (one Q4 case was reclassified as a non-attributable death under a pre-existing DNR/comfort-care order). The slide above was not updated before the packet froze. The accurate figure is 2; Quality will correct the slide in the next cycle.

## On mortality

Early pilot data are **encouraging but not statistically demonstrated**. The pilot was explicitly not powered to detect a mortality change, and no claim of mortality reduction is being made to the board at this time. We will report risk-adjusted mortality (O:E) at the next quarterly review once sufficient post-go-live volume has accrued.

## Open items

- Reconcile the two SEP-1 compliance measurement methods (manual abstraction vs. EHR flag) onto a single reported figure.
- Revisit a dedicated sepsis-nurse role in the FY2027 budget if the charge-nurse pager mechanism proves insufficient.

title: DRAFT — ED→ICU Sepsis Escalation Policy (Proposal A: Dedicated Sepsis Nurse)
text:
# DRAFT — ED→ICU Sepsis Escalation Policy (Proposal A: Dedicated Sepsis Nurse)

**Date:** March 20, 2026
**Status:** DRAFT proposal for committee discussion — NOT adopted
**Author:** Priyanka Rao, MD (ICU Director) and Janet Mwangi, RN (Nursing)

---

## Proposal

Establish a **dedicated sepsis nurse, one per shift**, on the ED and on 4West (a new 1.0 FTE per shift, ~3.0 FTE per unit across the rotation). The sepsis nurse would:

- Own the sepsis-alert response end to end.
- Place the time-zero orders, ensure antibiotic delivery within target, and shepherd the repeat-lactate draw.
- Be the single accountable person for bundle completion.

## Rationale

Bundle compliance fails today because no single person owns it; responsibility is diffuse across triage, the primary nurse, and the physician. A dedicated role removes that ambiguity.

## Resource implication

This requires net-new nursing FTE. Per the Nurse Staffing Policy (effective Jan 2025), any change to budgeted unit ratios must go through the Staffing Committee and is subject to the annual position-control budget. At ~6 FTE across two units, this is a material ask in a year with a frozen nursing budget.

## Open question for the committee

Can we fund 6 new FTE? If not, is there a no-new-FTE mechanism that still creates single-point accountability? *(See the adopted v2 escalation memo for the committee's answer.)*

title: ED→ICU Sepsis Escalation Policy (ADOPTED)
text:
# ED→ICU Sepsis Escalation Policy (ADOPTED)

**Date:** April 1, 2026
**Status:** ADOPTED — supersedes the March 20 draft proposal (Proposal A: Dedicated Sepsis Nurse)
**Authors:** Karen Holloway, MD; Janet Mwangi, RN; Priyanka Rao, MD
**Approved into Protocol v2.0 §6**

---

## Decision

The committee did **not** adopt the dedicated-sepsis-nurse proposal. The Nurse Staffing Policy's position-control freeze for FY2026 made ~6 net-new FTE infeasible, and the Staffing Committee declined to sponsor the request this cycle.

**Adopted instead:** a **sepsis-alert pager carried by the charge nurse** on each shift (ED and 4West). No net-new FTE. The charge nurse:

- Receives the sepsis-alert page on any positive screen with hypotension or lactate ≥ 4 mmol/L.
- Confirms time-zero orders are placed and antibiotic delivery is tracked to target.
- Escalates to the ICU resource nurse if a bed or higher level of care is needed.

## Trade-off acknowledged

Single-point accountability is weaker than under the dedicated-nurse proposal, because the charge nurse carries this alongside existing duties. The committee accepted this trade-off as the only option compatible with the FY2026 staffing budget, and will revisit a dedicated role in the FY2027 budget cycle if pilot data show the pager mechanism is insufficient.

## Reference

This policy operates within, and does not amend, the Nurse Staffing Policy (effective January 2025).

**Owner:** Chief Nursing Officer / Staffing Committee

## 1. Purpose

Define budgeted nurse-to-patient ratios, position control, and the process for any staffing change at Stillwater Regional Medical Center. This is the governing reference for all unit staffing decisions.

## 2. Budgeted ratios (medical-surgical and critical care)

- ICU: 1:2 (1:1 for unstable patients).
- Step-down / 4West: 1:4.
- ED: target 1:4, surge-adjusted.

Net-new nursing FTE may not be added outside the annual position-control budget. Any in-year request for new FTE must be sponsored by the Staffing Committee and offset within the approved nursing budget. **FY2026 operates under a position-control freeze**: no net-new nursing FTE absent CNO and CFO sign-off.

## 4. Standing nature

This policy is the durable reference for staffing decisions across all quality and operational initiatives. It is not specific to any one project and remains in force unless formally amended by the Staffing Committee.

title: Sepsis Response Protocol v1.0 (Adult)
text:
# Sepsis Response Protocol v1.0 (Adult)

**Date:** June 1, 2024
**Document type:** Clinical protocol — controlled document SR-CP-014
**Effective:** June 1, 2024
**Owner:** Department of Emergency Medicine
**Status header (as printed):** ACTIVE — supersedes the 2019 sepsis order set

---

## 1. Purpose

Standardize the recognition and initial management of adult patients with suspected sepsis at Stillwater Regional Medical Center.

## 2. Screening

Nurse-driven sepsis screening using the SIRS-based screening tool is **available and encouraged** at triage and on inpatient units. Completion is **not mandatory**; a positive screen prompts physician notification.

## 3. Antibiotic timing

For patients with suspected sepsis or septic shock, broad-spectrum antibiotics should be administered **within 3 hours** of the time of recognition ("time zero"). The 3-hour target applies uniformly to sepsis and septic shock.

## 4. Laboratory

- Serum lactate drawn at time zero.
- Blood cultures drawn before antibiotics where feasible.
- A **repeat lactate is not specified** by this protocol.

## 5. Fluids

Crystalloid 30 mL/kg for hypotension or lactate ≥ 4 mmol/L, within 3 hours.

## 6. Escalation

ED attending to consult Critical Care for refractory hypotension. No standing sepsis-alert paging mechanism is defined; escalation is by direct phone call.

## 7. Review cycle

Scheduled biennial review. (This document was overdue for review at the time the Sepsis Pathway 2.0 initiative was chartered.)

title: Sepsis Response Protocol v2.0 (Adult)
text:
# Sepsis Response Protocol v2.0 (Adult)

**Date:** April 20, 2026
**Document type:** Clinical protocol — controlled document SR-CP-014 (revision 2)
**Approved:** April 20, 2026 by the Quality & Patient Safety Committee
**Effective:** May 1, 2026
**Owner:** Sepsis Steering Committee (Emergency Medicine, Critical Care, ID/Stewardship, Nursing, Pharmacy)
**Status header (as printed):** ACTIVE — supersedes Sepsis Response Protocol v1.0 (June 2024)

---

## 1. Purpose

Replace Protocol v1.0 with a recognition-first, stratified pathway for adult sepsis and septic shock, incorporating the findings of the January 2026 sentinel-event root-cause analysis.

## 2. Screening — now mandatory

Nurse-driven sepsis screening is **mandatory** at ED triage and at every shift assessment on 4West and the ICU. A positive screen triggers the sepsis-alert pathway (see §6) and is documented as a discrete EHR field.

## 3. Antibiotic timing — stratified

The single 3-hour target of v1.0 is replaced by a stratified target:

- **Septic shock** (hypotension requiring vasopressors or lactate ≥ 4 mmol/L): broad-spectrum antibiotics **within 1 hour** of recognition.
- **Sepsis without shock:** antibiotics **within 3 hours** of recognition, with antimicrobial selection guided by the stewardship-endorsed empiric table (Appendix B).

This stratification was adopted explicitly to focus the 1-hour mandate on the population in which the evidence is strongest (shock), while avoiding a blanket 1-hour broad-spectrum mandate for undifferentiated sepsis. See the Antimicrobial Stewardship position memo (March 2026) for the rationale.

## 4. Laboratory

- Serum lactate at time zero.
- **Repeat lactate at 3 hours** if the initial value is ≥ 2 mmol/L (new in v2.0).
- Blood cultures before antibiotics.

## 5. Fluids

Crystalloid 30 mL/kg for hypotension or lactate ≥ 4 mmol/L, within 3 hours (unchanged from v1.0).

## 6. Escalation

A **sepsis-alert pager carried by the charge nurse** on each unit is activated on any positive screen with hypotension or lactate ≥ 4 mmol/L. (An earlier draft proposed a dedicated sepsis nurse per shift; that proposal was not adopted — see the escalation policy memo.)

## 7. Measurement

SEP-1 3-hour bundle compliance is the primary process measure. The committee notes that, at the time of approval, the two measurement methods (manual abstraction and the automated EHR flag) had **not yet been reconciled**, and compliance must be interpreted accordingly.

## 8. Review cycle

Annual review, or sooner on any sentinel event.

title: Antimicrobial Stewardship Position Memo — On a 1-Hour Antibiotic Mandate
text:
# Antimicrobial Stewardship Position Memo — On a 1-Hour Antibiotic Mandate

**Date:** March 6, 2026
**Author:** Elena Soto, MD — Infectious Disease; Chair, Antimicrobial Stewardship Program
**To:** Sepsis Steering Committee
**Re:** Proposed universal 1-hour door-to-antibiotic target

---

## Position

I support faster antibiotics for septic shock. I **do not support** a blanket 1-hour broad-spectrum antibiotic mandate applied to all patients with suspected sepsis, and I want the rationale on the record before the protocol is finalized.

## The evidence does not say what the proposal implies

Dr. Tran's proposal cites the association between earlier antibiotics and lower mortality. That association is **strongest, and arguably only robust, for septic shock**. The Surviving Sepsis Campaign's 2021 "1-hour bundle" recommendation was itself downgraded and remains contested precisely because the data for *undifferentiated, non-shock* sepsis are weak. There is **no high-quality evidence** that a 1-hour mandate reduces mortality in sepsis without shock.

## The harm of a blanket mandate is real and measurable

A universal 1-hour clock, enforced as a quality metric, predictably drives:

- Broad-spectrum antibiotics started on patients who turn out not to be infected (we already see this; our *C. difficile* rate and our carbapenem days-of-therapy are not trivial).
- Pressure to skip blood cultures or source assessment to "beat the clock."
- Anchoring on infection when the differential is still open.

These are not hypothetical; they are the documented downsides of time-to-antibiotic metrics in the stewardship literature. A mortality benefit that does not exist for non-shock sepsis cannot justify them.

## Recommendation

**Stratify.** 1-hour target for septic shock (where the evidence supports urgency); 3-hour target for sepsis without shock, with antimicrobial selection per the stewardship empiric table. This captures the benefit where it is real and avoids the harm where the benefit is not demonstrated.

I will support v2.0 if it stratifies. I will formally dissent if it imposes a universal 1-hour broad-spectrum mandate.
